lessons.title: OUTCH
intro: Our board is connected to a teletype: a typewriter the computer can type on. The KIM-1 has a routine in its ROM at $1EA0 called OUTCH (OUTput CHaracter). It prints the character in A.
Give the address a name first: OUTCH = $1EA0. That's a constant, not a label. Then JSR OUTCH prints.
Characters are numbers too. You can write them with a quote in front: LDA #'H loads the code of the letter H. On this board, OUTCH leaves A, X and Y unchanged (the real one wasn't so polite).

options: Prints the character in A on the teletype
Reads a key from the keypad
exercises.explanation: OUTCH is a subroutine in the KIM-1 ROM. It types the character in A.

exercises.prompt: Give the address $1EA0 the name OUTCH.
exercises.explanation: NAME = value defines a constant. A colon would make a label for the current line.

options: The character code of the letter Z
exercises.explanation: 'Z means "the code of the character Z".

exercises.prompt: This should print A, but nothing shows up on the teletype. Which line is in the wrong place?
exercises.explanation: OUTCH prints whatever is in A at that moment, and A is still 0. Load the letter first, then JSR OUTCH.
Define OUTCH first, then load and print each letter in order.

lessons.title: ASCII
intro: Which number is which character? The code is called ASCII. Capital letters run from 'A = $41 to 'Z = $5A, digits from '0 = $30 to '9 = $39, and a space is $20.
Because the letters are in order, you can do math with them: 'A + 1 is 'B. A loop that adds 1 prints the alphabet.
Two special codes: 13 starts a new line (carriage return), and 0 isn't printed at all. We'll use 0 as an end marker soon.

exercises.prompt: What is the ASCII code of 'A?
exercises.explanation: Capital letters start at $41. ($61 is the small a.)

exercises.prompt: What is the ASCII code of the digit '7?
exercises.explanation: Digits start at $30 for '0, so '7 is $30 + 7 = $37.
It starts at C and adds 1 after printing, three times: C, D, E.
13 is the carriage return. The teletype moves to the start of the next line.
$20 (32) is the space. $30 would print the digit 0.

exercises.prompt: This should print 12345, but it prints 1 five times. Which line is missing something after it?
exercises.explanation: A never changes, so the same digit is printed every round. After printing: CLC, ADC #1.

lessons.title: Messages
intro: Printing letter by letter gets long. Instead, put the whole text in a table: MSG: .BYTE "HELLO", 0. Text in double quotes becomes one byte per letter.
The 0 at the end marks where the message stops. A loop reads MSG,X, stops at the 0 with BEQ, and prints everything else.
This is the same loop you used for tables, with a different way to stop: not after a fixed count, but at the marker.

exercises.prompt: Why is there a 0 at the end of the message?
options: It marks the end, so the loop knows when to stop
The teletype needs it to start
exercises.explanation: LDA sets the Z flag when it loads the 0, and BEQ DONE leaves the loop.
H, I, ! and the 0: four bytes.

exercises.prompt: Leave the loop at the end marker.
exercises.explanation: LDA sets Z when it loads 0. BEQ jumps out of the loop then.
The loop prints every byte until the 0.

exercises.prompt: This program prints its message and then lots of garbage. Which line is missing something?
exercises.explanation: Without the 0 at the end, the loop keeps reading whatever comes after the message.
Start at entry 0, load, stop at the marker, print, next entry, repeat. The message goes at the very end.
